compose: recreate container when mounted image digest changes Until now, mustRecreate logic only checked for divergence in TypeVolume mounts but ignored TypeImage mounts. This inconsistency caused containers to erroneously retain stale images even after the source image was rebuilt. This commit updates ensureImagesExists to resolve image volume sources to their digests using the official reference package. This enables ServiceHash (config hash) to naturally detect underlying image digest changes, triggering recreation via the standard convergence logic. An E2E test case is added to verify this behavior. Fixes #13547

Replace sync.Once with sync.Mutex so that only successful version lookups are cached. Errors (context cancellation, network blips) are returned without caching, allowing subsequent calls to retry.

After API negotiation, Compose should only rely on the negotiated version and never use the daemon's raw max version for request shaping. Before API 1.44 (Docker Engine 25.0), ContainerCreate only accepted a single EndpointsConfig entry. Passing multiple entries silently drops all but one network, leaving containers under-connected on older daemons such as Docker 20.10 or Synology DSM 7.1/7.2.

For Docker daemons older than API 1.44, the extra networks omitted from ContainerCreate must be connected individually after creation via NetworkConnect. If any NetworkConnect call fails, remove the freshly created container to prevent orphans.

The model may declare jobs this runtime cannot execute yet. Commands that materialize the application warn about them, and refuse an active (profile-enabled) scheduled job before any resource is created — up, create and start alike: silently not scheduling would break expectations, while manual jobs just wait for an explicit trigger.

`docker compose run <job>` materializes the job — a ContainerSpec + WorkloadSpec, the same layers a service is made of — as a service for the one-off machinery: its profile is activated, the project narrowed to its dependencies by WithSelectedJob, and the exit code flows back.

Per the spec, any job can be triggered manually by an explicit run command, its automated triggers notwithstanding — so run now accepts scheduled jobs too. The exception is a job explicitly declared with triggers.manual: false, which run rejects: meant for scheduled jobs whose out-of-schedule execution would be harmful.

The unit suite ran without -race, so data races in the concurrent code paths (scheduler, watch, executor) were only caught if they happened to corrupt a result. Build the test stage with cgo (gcc + musl-dev) and pass -race to gotestsum. The suite is race-clean: 1100 tests, no report.

Every plan node acquired a concurrency slot before running, including OpWaitCondition, which then kept it for the whole health polling. An entry of the cache of extracted projects was taken as complete as soon as its directory existed, while the files were written into it one after the other. A run interrupted in the middle of an extraction, or another run that loads the same artifact at the same time, left a directory that was then used as it was, with some of the files missing.

When a run replaces a directory of the cache that is not a complete entry, it sets it aside before removing it, so that it does not remove the entry that another run has put in place in the meantime. The place it is set aside in is now a temporary directory of its own, so that two runs replacing the same entry at the same time never share one.

A run whose replacement of a directory that is not an entry failed put that directory back unconditionally. Another run having set aside the entry that took its place in the meantime, the directory put back stood in the way of the final rename of that run, whose deferred removal then deleted the complete entry it had set aside: the cache ended with the incomplete directory after a run returned su…

A commit was checked out directly into its directory of the cache, which was then taken for complete as soon as it existed: a run interrupted during the fetch or the checkout left a partial directory that every later run used.

The cache of remote resources now has one directory for each kind of resource: the checkouts of Git repositories are in "git", and the extracted OCI artifacts are in "oci" rather than at the root of the cache.

Get returned the manifest the registry served without checking it against the digest of the descriptor: the one of the reference when it is digested, the one the registry announces in Docker-Content-Digest when it is a tag. Neither is checked by containerd on this path, which doesn't go through its content store, and GetBlob already checks what it fetches for that reason.

An entry of the cache of extracted projects was taken as complete as soon as its directory, or a marker file in it, was there. An artifact chooses, through the annotations of its layers, the files it writes in that directory, so it can write a marker itself, and so did what releases that did not verify the manifests they fetched had cached there: neither proves that the directory is the extractio…

The media type a registry reports with a manifest is not authenticated, only the content is: a registry could serve the authentic bytes of an image index under the media type of a manifest, which was then read as one, extracted as nothing and cached as a complete entry that holds no compose file.

The dry-run client cannot attach to an exec, so any lifecycle hook reached under --dry-run (pre_stop on down/stop/restart, post_start on up/restart) made the command fail with "interactive exec is not supported in dry-run mode".

WithDryRun re-initializes the Docker CLI with fresh client options, whose empty log level makes Initialize reset logrus to info. Under --dry-run, --verbose was therefore dropped as soon as the backend was created, hiding every debug log of the operation.
Hooks are skipped silently under --dry-run. Log each skipped hook at debug level so --verbose shows which one would have run.

The documented contract of EventProcessor.Done is success == true when the operation succeeded, but Run was passing err != nil, so custom processors received an inverted value. No built-in writer uses the argument, which is why this went unnoticed.

A stopped container still refers to the networks it was attached to. When one of them was removed, up created the network again but started the old container, and the engine refused: "network <id> not found".

A pre_start hook container that fails to start (an executable missing from the image of the hook, a bad mount, ...) was reported with the bare error of the engine. It names neither the hook nor its image, and it surfaces on the row of the service container, so it reads as the service failing to start.

Without --detach, `up --wait` now attaches to the containers and streams their logs until the services are running|healthy, then ends the session and leaves them up. Until now --wait silently forced --detach, so a service failing to become healthy left no clue about why.
Once every attached container is gone the monitor ends the session, and with it the event loop that handles Ctrl+C: later interruptions are lost.

Describe the engine's jobs extension (org.mobyproject.jobs.v0) as a Go interface with its request and reply types, the generated gRPC client, and the mapping of its status codes to errdefs errors. moby/extensions is pinned to the version the engine vendors. Nothing uses it yet.

A job with a schedule is registered through the engine's jobs extension, which fires it on its own clock; create and up register it, up stays re-runnable since Create is idempotent on the spec hash, and a full down removes the jobs. The extension ships disabled by default and cannot be listed, so Compose probes it with a List scoped to the project; when the engine cannot run jobs, up, create and…

`docker compose run <job>` triggers a run of the job on the engine, starts its dependencies first, streams its logs and returns its exit code like a one-off service; a job accepts manual triggering unless it declares manual: false. A scheduled job runs as up registered it: an override, or a job up never registered, is refused. A manual job is removed from the engine after its run, so the next run…

Engines before 29.10 have no jobs extension, so the jobs scenarios that need it were always skipped. Add a leg on 29.10.0-rc.1 from the test channel with the extension enabled through daemon.json; the stable legs keep covering an engine without it.

up and create report each scheduled job like any other resource: created, or running when an identical job is already registered. A dry run used to say nothing about jobs, and run <job> returned without any output; it now starts the dependencies through the dry-run client and reports the run, without reaching the engine's jobs.
